analysis.one_liner: Raises federal tobacco taxes and spends part of the revenue on anti-smoking education, especially for youth.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 40 bipartisan cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died in committee when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have roughly raised every federal excise tax on tobacco — about 2.5 times the existing rates on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless and pipe tobacco — and created a new tax on cigarette rolling tobacco. Ten percent of the new revenue would fund a trust fund for public education on smoking hazards, including paid advertising, with special focus on keeping young people from starting. It also ordered a Treasury study of smoking's health care costs and how tax rates affect youth smoking.
analysis.who_benefits: The public, especially children, would gain from higher cigarette prices (which studies show discourage teen smoking) and from a sustained public education campaign on smoking hazards, funded by tobacco tax revenue rather than general taxes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, especially children and teens

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal cigarette excise tax from $8 and $16.80 per thousand to $20.50 and $43.05 per thousand, and increases taxes on cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, cigarette papers and tubes by similar multiples [S3].
Imposes a new $1.17-per-pound tax on cigarette rolling tobacco, closing a loophole for roll-your-own cigarettes [S3].

Creates a Smoking Cost Recovery and Education Trust Fund receiving 10% of the new tax revenue, to pay for school-age programs, minority health programs, and paid advertising on the hazards of smoking, aimed especially at youth [S3].
Requires an ongoing Treasury study, reported every two years, on smoking's health care costs, youth smoking rates, and how cigarette tax rates affect smoking by children [S3].

Tax increases of this kind are recognized as an effective way to reduce smoking, particularly among price-sensitive young smokers, per the bill's own design pairing the tax with the required youth-smoking study [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers — including adult low-income smokers, for whom the tax is a larger share of income — and the tobacco industry, which would face lower demand, plus tobacco-growing regions and retailers exposed to the new floor-stock tax on inventory.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco excise taxes are regressive: adult smokers, who disproportionately have lower incomes, would pay the higher tax on every pack whether or not they quit [S3].
The bill imposes a one-time floor-stock tax on tobacco inventory held by wholesalers and manufacturers as of October 1, 1989, though retail stocks are exempt [S3].
Higher tobacco taxes fall hardest on tobacco-farming and manufacturing regions, where jobs and local economies depend on tobacco sales.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains — fewer young smokers and a funded education campaign — would likely outweigh the cost, since the tax falls on a product that imposes large health care costs on everyone. The main honest objection is fairness: the tax is paid by low-income smokers, and only 10% of the new revenue goes to education while the rest enters general revenue. It would have been better designed to direct more of the revenue to the programs it justifies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Andrews introduced the bill on January 31, 1989, joined by 15 original cosponsors including Reps. Stark, Waxman, Synar, and Roukema [S3].
It was referred the same day to both the Ways and Means Committee (which handles taxes) and the Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].
On February 13, 1989, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment [S5].
The bill attracted 40 cosponsors, 34 Democrats and 6 Republicans, but neither committee ever reported it, and it received no floor action before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and retailers were better off: no tax increase ever took effect and no anti-smoking ad campaign was ever funded. Smokers continued paying the old, lower federal tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies, which faced no tax increase

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 34 Democrats and 6 Republicans cosponsored — but no vote was ever taken, so the party split on the bill's merits was never tested [S4].

industries.note: The bill would raise excise taxes on all tobacco products roughly 2.5-fold and add a tax on roll-your-own tobacco, directly cutting demand for their products. The industry benefits from the bill's death: prices stayed lower and no government-funded anti-smoking advertising was created [S3].
The bill imposed a one-time floor-stock tax on untaxed tobacco inventory held on October 1, 1989, though retail store stocks were exempt [S3].

industries.industry: Tobacco growers and tobacco-dependent local economies
industries.note: Higher taxes would reduce demand for leaf tobacco in growing regions, a cost concentrated in a few communities rather than spread nationally.
